claim: The paper's statement that its throughput gain extends to larger mixture-of-experts models (Qwen3-235B-A22B, DeepSeek-V3 and Kimi-K2.6) is not established, because those speedups were measured on copies of the models with random weights, whose routers do not send tokens to the experts the trained models would choose, and the inter-node traffic that the speedup comes from depends on exactly those routing choices.
evidence: Section 5.4 is headed "The implementation and throughput gain extends to larger MoE architectures" and reports 1.15x, 1.18x and 1.05x throughput on Qwen3-235B-A22B, DeepSeek-V3 and Kimi-K2.6, adding that "these tests use full-sized models with random weights and report throughput improvements only." Appendix G.4 repeats that "These full-sized architectures use random weights" and that the comparisons establish "execution cost and memory feasibility, without assessing task performance after adaptation." The traffic being saved is routing-dependent: Equation (1) makes inter-node volume proportional to the average number of remote nodes each token reaches, and Appendix F.1 measures that quantity from routing traces, "routed transfers reach 2.73 remote nodes per token on average" for the trained Qwen3-30B-A3B, noting that the estimates "remain fixed for a given configuration, topology and routing trace." A randomly initialised router produces a different trace, so the larger-model numbers show neither the accuracy cost of the compression on those models nor the traffic, and hence the speedup, under their real routing.
